newsitem.title: USA: Coast Guard maintains restrictions on Mississippi.
newsitem.headline: Coast Guard maintains restrictions on Mississippi.

text.p: A grain freighter accident on the lower Mississippi earlier today did not disrupt maritime traffic, but conditions on the flood-swollen river remain hazardous, Coast Guard officials said.

In the latest of a string of mishaps on the fast-running Mississippi, a vessel carrying some 23,000 tonnes of grain lost power and plowed into a petroleum coke facility near New Orleans early Wednesday.

The El Salvador-bound Tzanetis was carrying a cargo of corn, wheat and rice, industry operators said. While the vessel reportedly suffered only minor harm, the dock, owned by CII Carbon, was extensively damaged.
"It's not affecting traffic at all," said Commander Ken Parris of the Coast Guard's Marine Safety Office in New Orleans.
While the cause of the accident was still under investigation, the fast river conditions appeared to be a "major contributing factor", he said.

The Coast Guard was unable to predict when the vessel would be released, but said that a crane barge would need to be brought alongside the Tzanetis to remove conveyor equipment that had fallen onto the ship's deck during the collision.

Meanwhile, navigational restrictions imposed last week on petroluem product and chemical ships remain in place, Parris said, and would not be relaxed until the height of the river drops substantially.
The water level was retreating at a rate of about one-tenth of a foot per day, and had come down half a foot since cresting last week, he said.

"It is very difficult to estimate due to the vagaries of the weather," Parris said. "We have about another two-and-a-half to three feet to go before we will even examine relaxing any restrictions. At (this) rate, it will be a while."

The transit restrictions, which include a sharp cut on tugboat loads and a limit on deep-draft chemical and petroluem product ships to daylight transit only, have resulted in a backlog of about 30 vessels each day, Parris said.
"You end up with a queue of 30 vessels each night waiting to continue downbound at sunrise," he said.

But in a sign the worst may be over for the Mississippi, the Army Corps of Engineers said it had begun closing the Bonnet Carre Spillway on Wednesday. The spillway, which is located 33 miles north of New Orleans, had been opened several weeks ago to slow the river's flow and prevent flooding farther downriver.
An Army Corps spokesman estimated it would take 10 days to two weeks to shut the spillway completely.
((-- W Pollack, New York Commodities Desk +1 212 859 1640))
